primary_claim: In Qwen-2.5 1.5B Instruct, echo/repeat tasks are resolved through an MLP-heavy circuit rather than late attention, with attention head 2 at the token-emergence layer consistently ranking among the top-3 most important heads across ablation experiments on 44 words and both prompt phrasings, and attending strongly (~90%) to the BOS token, likely as an attention sink.

effect.metric: consistency of head 2 ranking top-3 in zero-ablation logit-drop experiments
effect.value: head 2 always in top-3 heads across 44 words and both 'repeat'/'echo' prompt phrasings

contradicts_or_qualifies: Ablation results and Direct Logit Attribution (DLA) results disagree strongly for this task, implying most of the processing happens in the MLP layer rather than being visible via late-layer attention DLA alone
stated_future_work: Continue with ARENA and study sparse autoencoders as a mechanistic interpretability tool
Further investigate the diverging cosine-similarity results and the BOS attention-sink hypothesis, e.g. using mean ablation
Record how each head changes logits for non-target tokens, not just the target token, to disentangle 'which word' vs. 'repeat/print' information
Read more mechanistic interpretability literature, e.g. 'In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors' by Hendel, Geva, and Globerson
limitations_stated: Only measured logit change on the target token (e.g. 'cat'), not the absolute change across all tokens, so ablations that raised another token's score above the target weren't captured
Writing Notebook 2 by having Claude extract and apply the Notebook 1 pipeline felt too detached from the code, a workflow the author decided not to repeat
Forgot to confirm the BOS-attention-focus hypothesis with data before writing up (later confirmed it held)
quote: My most interesting discovery is that ablation results and DLA results disagree strongly in this task.
